query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The native passive oxide film on as-received Q235 steel undergoes a thermally activated phase transformation under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. This transformation alters its microstructure—either densifying it into a more protective crystalline layer or promoting porous, void-rich areas due to selective elemental dissolution—thus changing its corrosion protection behavior relative to room‐temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received state with its native (pre-exposure) passive oxide film
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to an aggressive salt environment (e.g., Na2SO4) under controlled conditions at room temperature and separately under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C)
generation.conditions: Two regimes: (a) ambient temperature exposure where no thermal activation occurs and the oxide remains largely amorphous, and (b) high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) where heat triggers oxide phase crystallization and possible phase separation. A reference sample with a known, stable protective coating may be used to benchmark results.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the oxide layer’s structure (transition from amorphous to crystalline or porous morphologies, including changes in grain boundaries and elemental distribution) as induced by thermal activation
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the as-formed native oxide film is relatively amorphous and self-limiting, effectively retarding corrosion. However, at 700–900 °C, thermal energy induces re-crystallization and phase separation in the oxide; this can either result in a denser, more protective crystalline oxide (if densification occurs) or in a porous, degraded layer (if voids form due to selective elemental dissolution), thereby modulating the corrosion rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under room temperature conditions, low corrosion rates will be observed with little to no oxide structural change. In contrast, high-temperature exposure will show measurable oxide structural evolution via in situ EIS and Raman spectroscopy, corresponding either to improved protection (if a denser crystalline phase forms) or to accelerated degradation (if the oxide becomes porous), relative to the room temperature reference.
generation.baseline: Corrosion performance of as-received Q235 steel at room temperature in the same salt environment, maintaining an intact, amorphous native oxide layer
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply only to Q235 steel in its as-received state under an oxygen-containing and salt-rich environment. The hypothesis may not hold if the oxide film is pre-enhanced by additional coatings or if exposure conditions (e.g., oxygen levels, salt composition, or duration) significantly differ from the controlled experimental parameters.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the thermally induced oxide transformation will predominantly yield a denser, self-healing protective film or a degraded, porous layer; the net effect likely depends on the precise thermal history, salt chemistry, and exposure duration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple as-received Q235 steel samples and subject them to identical aggressive salt exposure tests at room temperature and at 700–900 °C. Use in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) coupled with Raman spectroscopy during exposure to monitor the oxide film evolution. Post-exposure, perform cross-sectional SEM, XRD, and mass loss measurements to compare oxide phase, morphology, and corrosion rates between the two regimes and against a reference sample with a stable protective coating.
measurements: In situ EIS data to track changes in corrosion resistance
Raman spectra to identify phase changes in the oxide layer
XRD patterns and SEM images for oxide crystallinity and porosity
Mass loss and/or corrosion rate measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data show no significant difference in the oxide film’s structure or corrosion behavior between room-temperature and high-temperature exposures, or if no correlation exists between oxide phase transformation and corrosion rates, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

As can be seen from the data presented, in the case of Nb alloy samples after thermal testing, the surface is a mixture of an oxide film, the thickness of which is at least 500–700 nm in the case of the original sample and somewhat less (no more than 500 nm) in the case of the irradiated sample. At the same time, the structure of this oxide film for the original sample and the irradiated one has obvious differences. In the case of the initial sample, the oxidized layer is represented by a mixture of grain inclusions that make up the porous film, while for the irradiated samples, the oxide film delamination is observed with the formation of extended voids. When vanadium, tantalum, and titanium were added to the niobium alloy, the formation of oxide inclusions was not observed as a result of high-temperature tests. With an increasing N2 flow rate, the film deposited at a RN of 50% had the highest hardness (12.4 GPa), the highest modulus (169 GPa), a small roughness, and a beautiful color. The thicknesses of the films were gradually reduced from 298.8 nm to 200 nm, and all the thin films were of amorphous structure. NbTiAlSiZrNx HEA films prepared at N2 flow rates of 20%, 40%, and 50% were more corrosion-resistant than 304 SS. chosen.why: This move is most directly aligned with the research question by isolating the governing cause of corrosion protection failure or persistence via the temperature-dependent behavior of passive oxide layers. It leverages standard techniques in corrosion science to probe mechanistic changes across temperature regimes, thereby addressing the literature gap that has focused mainly on phenomenological performance rather than mechanistic understanding.

frame.system: Q235 carbon steel in its pre-exposure (as-received) state
frame.goal: Establish a mechanistic explanation for why corrosion protection degrades or is retained under both ambient and high‐temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt exposure regimes.
frame.limitation: Prior studies emphasized improvements in performance (hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or mass change) for specific materials and did not determine the underlying cause of protection persistence or failure across different temperature regimes. In particular, mechanistic links – especially combining aspects like HEA behavior, annealing effects, and hot-corrosion outcomes – remain minimally explored.
root_cause_cues: why corrosion protection persists or fails

A controlled study design must isolate the governing cause relative to an appropriate reference material.

Supporting evidence should be aligned with earlier observations on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels.

frame.regime: Testing must include both room-temperature exposure and high-temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt (e.g., Na2SO4 or mixed salt) environments, with controlled thermal and chemical conditions (including controlled annealing if needed).
prior_attempts: Studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels focused on performance metrics (improved hardness, wear resistance, reduced mass change) without mechanistic insights.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels (and, by extension, on HEAs) moved from reporting improved performance metrics such as hardness, wear resistance, and mass loss to beginning to probe the chemical and phase‐evolution changes during aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures. In particular, researchers documented that selective elemental dissolution (e.g. Mn loss) could favor the retention of protective species (e.g. Cr) and that thermal exposures promote phase precipitation. However, these works focused on performance and microstructural snapshots rather than dynamically correlating how an existing native oxide or passive film responds to high-temperature annealing and aggressive salt attack under both room‐ and high‐temperature regimes.
decision.unsolved: The underlying mechanistic link on Q235 steel – namely, how the native/passive oxide scale formed in the as-received (pre-exposure) state evolves under room-temperature and 700–900 °C salt environments, and thereby governs the retention or breakdown of corrosion protection – remains unestablished. In other words, it is still unknown whether thermal activation induces a self-healing or detrimental transformation in the oxide films and what microstructural features dictate this behavior.
decision.lever: temperature regime using in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) coupled with Raman spectroscopy
decision.why: Following the trend of shifting focus from indirect performance metrics to more insight‐driven studies, a controlled variable experiment that monitors the evolution of the native/passive oxide film is a natural next step. By exposing as-received Q235 steel to identical aggressive salt atmospheres at room temperature versus 700–900 °C and tracking the oxide’s chemical and structural evolution in situ, the study can directly test the hypothesis that thermally induced annealing effects (which may heal or degrade the oxide layer) govern the observed differences in corrosion behavior. This approach directly occupies the niche of addressing 'unexplained behaviour' by isolating the impact of temperature on corrosion mechanisms, as flagged by earlier papers.
